passage:
Monday: Nilesh wrote, "I like dogs. Dogs are nice." Trisha, his teacher, wrote beside it: "Why?"
Wednesday: He added, "Dogs are loyal. They play with you. They guard the house." Trisha circled "loyal" and wrote, "Tell me more."
Friday: His paragraph read, "Dogs are the best pets. First, they are loyal and wait for you at the door. Second, they play games. Finally, they guard the house at night. That is why I think every family should have a dog." Trisha gave him a gold star.

qa.q: What did Trisha write beside Nilesh's first sentences?
qa.a: Trisha wrote "Why?"

qa.q: What does Nilesh adding reasons suggest about how he felt about Trisha's questions?
qa.a: It suggests he felt encouraged and motivated by her questions, so he kept adding reasons to explain his opinion better.

qa.q: What helped Nilesh write an organised paragraph?
qa.a: Trisha's short questions pushed him to add reasons, then order them with first, second and finally.

qa.q: How might a reader feel reading Friday's paragraph?
qa.a: They would understand Nilesh's opinion clearly and might even agree with him.

grounding: It shows a child learning to write an organised paragraph supporting an opinion with reasons over days.

passage: "Omkar, you think writing is hard? When I started as a reporter, my editor tore up my first story. He said, 'You wrote your feelings, not your reasons.' So he taught me three steps: say it, prove it, finish it. Say what you think. Prove it with two or three reasons. Finish by saying it again, a little differently. I wrote every story like that for years. So for your essay on school holidays, what's your opinion?" Swati Mausi pushed a notebook across. "Now, prove it."

qa.q: What did Swati's editor do to her first story?
qa.a: He tore up her first story.

qa.q: What might Swati have felt when her editor tore up her story?
qa.a: She may have felt hurt and embarrassed, but she learned from it.

qa.q: What three steps does Swati teach Omkar?
qa.a: Say it, prove it, finish it: state your opinion, give reasons and end by restating it.

qa.q: How might Omkar feel hearing this story?
qa.a: Omkar might feel less afraid of mistakes and more ready to try the essay.

grounding: An elder tells a story teaching how to write organised paragraphs supporting an opinion with reasons.

passage: The essay on school uniforms was due in twenty minutes, and the laptop battery showed ten percent. Tejas panicked. Seema, his mother, said, "Write your opinion first." He typed: "I think school uniforms are good." "Why?" "Because everyone looks equal." "Another?" "It saves time in the morning." "One more?" "It shows we belong to one school." He added a closing line and hit save just as the screen went black. "Saved!" he shouted.

qa.q: What percentage did the laptop battery show?
qa.a: It showed ten percent.

qa.q: What does Tejas shouting "Saved!" suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he felt huge relief that his work was done in time.

qa.q: How did Seema help Tejas organise his essay?
qa.a: She asked him to state his opinion first and then asked "Why?" to draw out reasons.

qa.q: What would change if the battery had died earlier?
qa.a: He would have lost his work and felt more stress before the deadline.

grounding: It shows a child writing an opinion paragraph with reasons under time pressure.

passage:
Nitin, eleven, had to write a paragraph for school: "Should our school have a library period?" He wrote, "Yes. Library is nice," and pushed his notebook to his mother, Vandana, at the dining table of their Delhi flat.

She read it. "Why is it nice?"

He thought. "Because we can read books we choose. And... the classroom is noisy, the library is quiet. And some kids don't have books at home."

"Those are three reasons. Can they go in your paragraph?"

Nitin rewrote it: an opening sentence saying yes, three reasons with "first," "also," and "finally," and a last line. It filled half a page. He read it aloud, surprised at how convincing he sounded.

qa.q: How many reasons did Nitin give for a library period?
qa.a: He gave three reasons.

qa.q: How did Nitin feel when he read his new paragraph aloud?
qa.a: He felt surprised and pleased at how convincing he sounded.

qa.q: What did Vandana do that helped Nitin improve his writing?
qa.a: She asked "Why?" so he came up with his own reasons, then suggested putting them into the paragraph.

qa.q: How might Nitin's teacher see the rewritten paragraph?
qa.a: The teacher would likely see a clear opinion backed by organised reasons, much stronger than the first try.

grounding: Shows a child learning to write an organised paragraph supporting an opinion with reasons.

passage:
"Aparna Bua, I'm writing that flats should allow pets," Gurpreet, ten, said.

"Good. Why?"

"Because pets are cute."

"Is that enough to convince the building committee?"

Gurpreet frowned. "Maybe not. Okay... pets make people less lonely. Especially old people."

"Good. What else?"

"Children learn responsibility. And if owners clean up, there's no mess."

"And someone who disagrees?"

"They'd say dogs bark. So I'll say owners should train them."

Aparna nodded. "Now you have a real opinion paragraph."

Gurpreet started writing, counting reasons on her fingers.

qa.q: What was Gurpreet's first reason for allowing pets?
qa.a: Her first reason was that pets are cute.

qa.q: What does Gurpreet's frown suggest when Aparna Bua asks if that is enough?
qa.a: It suggests she felt unsure about her first reason and a little challenged, realising it was weak and she had to think harder.

qa.q: What did Aparna Bua do well in helping Gurpreet?
qa.a: She kept asking questions, including about the other side, so Gurpreet built stronger reasons herself.

qa.q: How might someone on the building committee react to Gurpreet's paragraph?
qa.a: They might take it more seriously because it has solid reasons and answers the barking worry.

grounding: A dialogue shows a child building an opinion paragraph with reasons and answering a counterargument.

passage:
In Class 6 our teacher asked us to write a paragraph: “Should school start later?” I'm Rafiq, and I thought it would be easy. I wrote, “Yes, because I'm sleepy.” That was it.
Ms Gurleen gave it back with a note: “Why? Give three reasons. Start with your opinion. End by saying it again.”
So I tried again. I wrote my opinion first. Then three reasons: children would be less sleepy, there would be less traffic at seven, and we could eat breakfast properly. Then I finished with my opinion again.
It was the first time a paragraph felt like a building instead of a pile of bricks.

qa.q: What did Rafiq write the first time?
qa.a: “Yes, because I'm sleepy.”

qa.q: How did Rafiq feel when the paragraph finally worked?
qa.a: Rafiq felt proud and satisfied, as if the paragraph was a building instead of a pile of bricks.

qa.q: What did Ms Gurleen's note teach Rafiq?
qa.a: It showed how to organise a paragraph: opinion first, three reasons, then the opinion again.

qa.q: How might Ms Gurleen feel reading Rafiq's second paragraph?
qa.a: Ms Gurleen is likely pleased to see the advice used and the argument made clearly.

grounding: An eleven-year-old learns to write an organised opinion paragraph with reasons.

passage:
Teacher's note, Class 5 English. Gopika Nair.
Lakshmi (ten) wrote her best paragraph yet this week, on “Our school should have a vegetable garden.”
She opened with her opinion in one clear sentence. Then three reasons: children would learn how food grows, the canteen could use the vegetables, and it would give shy children a quiet job. She even wrote “Some people may say it's too much work, but…” and answered it. She ended by repeating her opinion.
When I read it aloud, she went pink but kept her chin up.
Next step: I'll send her paragraph to the principal with her permission.

qa.q: What was Lakshmi's paragraph about?
qa.a: “Our school should have a vegetable garden.”

qa.q: How did Lakshmi feel when her paragraph was read aloud?
qa.a: She felt shy and embarrassed, but also proud, keeping her chin up.

qa.q: What made Lakshmi's paragraph strong?
qa.a: She stated her opinion, gave three reasons, answered an objection and ended by repeating her opinion.

qa.q: How might the principal react to Lakshmi's paragraph?
qa.a: The principal may be impressed and take the idea of a school garden seriously.

grounding: A teacher notes a ten-year-old writing a well-organised opinion paragraph with reasons.

passage:
Thursday
Today in English we had to write an opinion paragraph: “Should pets be allowed in school?” I said YES. Pranav said NO. We argued the whole lunch break.
So I wrote mine properly. Opinion first. Then reasons: pets teach kindness, they help nervous children feel calm, and we could take turns feeding them. Then Pranav's point: pets are messy. I answered it: we could have a rota for cleaning. Last sentence, my opinion again.
Pranav read it and said, “Okay, the rota is a good point.” Then he said he still says no.
I felt like a lawyer. — Noor

qa.q: What did Noor answer to Pranav's point that pets are messy?
qa.a: Noor said they could have a rota for cleaning.

qa.q: How did Noor feel after writing the paragraph?
qa.a: Noor felt confident and proud, like a lawyer.

qa.q: What made Noor's paragraph persuasive?
qa.a: It gave clear reasons, answered the other side's point and ended with the opinion again.

qa.q: How might Pranav feel after reading Noor's paragraph?
qa.a: Pranav may feel partly convinced by the rota idea, while still holding his own view.

grounding: A twelve-year-old writes an organised opinion paragraph and answers an objection.

passage:
The panchayat was deciding whether to turn the old store-room at the village school into a library. The teacher asked each child to write a paragraph: yes or no, and why.
Madhav wrote: "Yes. Library is good." Then he stopped.
Lokesh leaned over. "That's one line. Why is it good?"
Madhav chewed his pencil. He added: "First, we have only our textbooks at home. Second, in the rains we can't play outside, so we can read. Third, my little sister can learn to read before she goes to school."
He ended: "That is why the store-room should be a library."
Lokesh read it and nodded. "Now it's a real reason paragraph."

qa.q: What did Madhav write at first?
qa.a: "Yes. Library is good."

qa.q: What was Madhav feeling when he chewed his pencil?
qa.a: Madhav felt stuck and unsure how to explain why the library was good.

qa.q: How did Lokesh's question help Madhav's writing?
qa.a: Asking "Why is it good?" pushed Madhav to add three clear reasons and a closing line.

qa.q: How might the panchayat members see Madhav's paragraph?
qa.a: They might find it convincing because it gives real reasons from village life, not just an opinion.

grounding: A village child learns to support his opinion with reasons in a paragraph.

passage:
In Dublin, Liam's homework was to write an opinion paragraph. He chose "Dogs are better than cats."
His sister Nadia, who had a cat, read it. "You just wrote 'Dogs are the best' five times."
Liam scowled. "Because they are."
"Then prove it. Give reasons."
Liam thought. "Okay. One, dogs come for walks with you. Two, they can help people, like guide dogs. Three, they're happy when you come home."
"Better," said Nadia. "Still wrong, but better."
Liam wrote the three reasons, each with an example, and finished: "So I think dogs make better pets."

qa.q: What did Liam write five times at first?
qa.a: "Dogs are the best."

qa.q: What was Liam feeling when he scowled?
qa.a: Liam felt annoyed and defensive when Nadia criticised his paragraph.

qa.q: What made Liam's paragraph stronger?
qa.a: He gave three reasons, each with an example, and ended with a clear opinion sentence.

qa.q: How does Nadia see Liam's paragraph by the end?
qa.a: Nadia still disagrees with his opinion, but she thinks his writing is better because it has reasons.

grounding: A child in Ireland learns to back up an opinion with reasons.

passage:
In the Class 6 writing lesson, students swapped paragraphs to review. Lokesh got Jahnavi's, and Jahnavi got his.
Lokesh's said: "Our school should have a longer lunch break. It would be nice. Everyone wants it."
Jahnavi wrote in the margin: "Why would it be nice? Who is everyone?"
Lokesh read it and felt his face heat up. Then he looked at Jahnavi's paragraph. It had a topic sentence, three reasons, and an ending.
He rewrote his: "First, many of us don't finish eating. Second, we'd have time to play and then focus better. Third…"
He handed it back to her with a small nod.

qa.q: What did Jahnavi write in the margin?
qa.a: "Why would it be nice? Who is everyone?"

qa.q: What was Lokesh feeling when his face heated up?
qa.a: Lokesh felt embarrassed that his paragraph had no real reasons.

qa.q: How could the teacher use this kind of peer review again?
qa.a: The teacher could keep having students ask each other "why?" questions so they learn to add reasons.

qa.q: How might Jahnavi feel when Lokesh hands back the rewritten paragraph?
qa.a: Jahnavi probably feels respected, seeing that her comments helped him improve.

grounding: During peer review, a child learns to organise a paragraph and support his opinion.

passage:

passage:
Preeti, you want to know why I write letters to the newspaper? It started when I was eleven, during the Pongal holidays.
I, Yogesh, was angry that the colony park was locked. My father said, "Write it down. But give reasons, not just anger."
I wrote: the park should open because children need to play, old people need to walk, and it's our park. I ended: please open it before the holidays end.
The colony committee read it at the meeting. They opened it for evenings.
That's when I learned: an opinion with reasons can change things. So, Preeti, write yours.

qa.q: What did Yogesh's letter ask?
qa.a: To open the park before the holidays end.

qa.q: How did Yogesh feel about the locked park?
qa.a: Yogesh felt angry that the colony park was locked.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Yogesh's story?
qa.a: The father's advice to give reasons, not just anger, which made Yogesh's letter convincing.

qa.q: How might the colony committee have felt reading it?
qa.a: They likely felt impressed and persuaded by an eleven-year-old's reasons.

grounding: An elder recalls learning as a child to write an opinion supported by reasons.

passage:
The summer heat was so bad that the power went off at 2 pm, and Madhav's essay was due the next morning. His topic: "Should our school start at 9 instead of 7:30?"
The fan stopped. Sweat dripped onto his notebook. His friend Omkar, sitting with him on the balcony, groaned. "Just write 'yes, because sleep' and finish."
Madhav shook his head. "Miss said three reasons, with examples."
By the light of the window, he wrote: first, children sleep better; second, fewer kids skip breakfast; third, buses would miss the worst morning traffic. He ended with, "Some parents work early, so the school could keep a morning room open."
Omkar read it. "Okay, that's actually convincing."

qa.q: What time did the power go off?
qa.a: The power went off at 2 pm.

qa.q: What was Madhav feeling when Omkar told him to just write 'yes, because sleep'?
qa.a: Madhav felt determined and a bit stubborn, wanting to do the essay properly even in the heat.

qa.q: Which part of Madhav's paragraph made it stronger, and why?
qa.a: Adding a point for parents who work early made it stronger, because it answered a likely objection instead of ignoring it.

qa.q: How does Omkar's view of the essay change?
qa.a: Omkar first wants a quick answer, but after reading it he is impressed and finds it actually convincing.

grounding: Shows a child writing an organised paragraph that supports an opinion with reasons, under a hot power cut.
